messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol Ortega is a 27-year-old HVAC technician who came to treatment after months of telling herself she should be able to handle this on her own. She had always taken pride in being steady in difficult environments, moving through apartment basements, service corridors, rooftops, and cramped utility rooms with the confidence that came from knowing her trade. The trauma she described happened during a job call the previous year, when she was lured into a locked back room at a small commercial property by a woman who had seemed to be asking for help with the building’s cooling system. Inside, Marisol was restrained, trapped, and deliberately hurt over a period of hours. What stayed with her most vividly was not only the pain but the unbearable fact that a woman had gained her trust so easily, spoken calmly while injuring her, and controlled when she could move, speak, or hope the ordeal would end.

In the weeks afterward, Marisol found that certain moments in daily life acquired a force she could not explain away. Being alone with women, especially in enclosed work areas, made her body tense before she had fully registered why. If a tenant opened a door and she noticed a bandaged hand, a cut across knuckles, or bruising on exposed skin, she felt a rush of alarm and an urge to leave. The worst situations were the ordinary job conditions that left her with no easy exit—narrow mechanical closets, locked utility rooms, a customer standing between her and the door. She had come to believe that you can never know who will harm you, and because she no longer trusted herself to judge correctly, female clients and small signs of injury took on a threatening meaning quickly, as if they might reveal danger she was liable to miss until it was too late. That belief changed what caught and held her attention: things she might once have registered and dismissed—a woman pausing in a doorway, a hand hidden in a pocket, the click of a lock—now snagged immediately as reminders that demanded a response.

Once those moments were activated, Marisol shifted almost immediately into scanning and checking. She began making repeated rounds of her apartment each night, testing locks and windows, sometimes more than once, unable to settle until she had physically touched each one. She woke abruptly in the dark and walked the apartment to make sure she was still safe. At work she startled hard at footsteps behind her or the metallic slam of a service door. Already running at that pitch of alarm, she found that ordinary cues turned into warnings with very little provocation; once she felt threatened, closed rooms, women standing too near, or the sight of an unexplained injury seemed to leap forward as if the world were crowded with signs she had to read. Being cornered by a job layout or left alone with a woman in a back room could set this off fast; her attention narrowed to exits, keys, whether a door latched, whether anyone else knew where she was. The checking made sense to her because she was certain harm could come without warning, and because she doubted her own judgment, she felt she had to compensate by staying vigilant at all times. Living with that level of danger in her body became, in its own way, evidence to her that the assault had permanently changed her and that the world really was a place where she could not afford to let herself feel unguarded.

Her memories of the assault were difficult to speak about directly. When they came, they carried intense shame, as if recalling it exposed something disgraceful about her rather than something done to her. At times the memory felt strangely unreal, almost as though it had happened to somebody else and she was looking at it from a distance; at other times it broke through with such force that she had to stop talking, leave the room, or shut down the thought altogether because the emotion was too much. When that memory broke through, the danger no longer felt finished or in the past; for several minutes afterward she moved as if the threat were physically present again, bracing in her own apartment or at a job site as though she were still trapped and being watched. Those reactions were tied closely to what she had come to think about herself. Marisol was haunted by the belief that she had permanently changed for the worse, that something in her had been damaged beyond repair, and that remembering the event proved how weak or compromised she had become. The more she interpreted the trauma this way, the more alien and shame-filled the memory felt, and the less able she was to stay with it.

The memory also sharpened the world around her. Seeing someone’s wounds could call up flashes of the assault so abruptly that she felt she was back in the room, and after nights of waking alert and checking locks she was even more sensitive the next day to closed spaces and blocked exits. A female customer lingering too close while she worked inside an equipment closet could make her think, before anything had happened, that she had no options. She started changing how she handled service calls, asking coworkers to accompany her on certain jobs, lingering near doorways, and turning down assignments in residential settings where she might be alone. That had begun to affect her standing at work; she worried colleagues noticed her hesitations, and this fed the conviction that she no longer trusted herself to do the right thing under pressure.

Over time, the vigilance itself deepened her despair. Marisol saw the nightly checking, the jolts of startle, and the inability to relax as proof that she was no longer the person she had been. Each awakening to inspect the locks seemed to confirm that the world was unsafe and that she was permanently altered by what happened. By the time she sought help, she was exhausted and frightened by how small her life had become. She came in after leaving a job midway through when she was alone in a locked mechanical room with a female property manager and noticed a fresh cut on the woman’s forearm; Marisol’s heart began pounding, she could not think, and she walked off the site. What frightened her most was the sense that the danger was everywhere and that she could no longer trust herself to know the difference. What she most hoped for was not to erase the event, but to stop living as if she were still trapped inside it.
